title: China’s Overcapacity Has a Mind of Its Own
text:
China’s Overcapacity Has a Mind of Its Own

Foreign Policy

Adek Berry/AFP/Getty Images

The following is an excerpt from an op-ed published in Foreign Policy on October 26, 2026, written by Lizzi C. Lee, Fellow on Chinese Economy at ASPI's Center for China Analysis, and Xiao Ma, associate professor of political science at Peking University. There is no sign that China’s export juggernaut is slowing down. China’s auto exports, for example, have grown more than tenfold since 2020 and are estimated to reach 10 million vehicles this year. The country posted a record trade surplus of $119.1 billion in August alone, putting it on track to surpass the $1.2 trillion surplus of 2025. The “China shock” is now an everyday reality in multiple sectors, from electric vehicles to power generation.Accusations that China is exporting excess capacity have echoed across the United States, the European Union, and Southeast Asia, though China has vehemently rejected this. The concerns are understandable: It is hard to compete with Chinese industrial might, and local industry stakeholders worry about everything from job losses to dependence on Chinese suppliers.But the conventional view that China’s dominant position in the global market is the result of the central government’s long-term strategic planning and top-down industrial policy tells only half the story. Beijing is not fully in control of the bulldozer of Chinese manufacturing, and the results have sometimes been far beyond what the government wanted or planned for.Read the full op-ed here.
